analysis.one_liner: Bars federal regulations from taking effect until Congress passes each one as a law.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 67 House members including only 2 Democrats, never left a House Judiciary subcommittee and received no committee or floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under this bill, no federal regulation would take effect until both the House and Senate passed a bill made up of the regulation's exact text and the President signed it. Agencies would still write rules, but each one would need an act of Congress to become binding. Because agencies issue thousands of rules a year and Congress passes only a few hundred laws, the practical effect would be that most new regulations die by default. The bill created a fast-track process — no committee referral, one hour of debate, a vote within 60 days — to make that mass of votes technically possible.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses and other regulated parties gain the most: any rule they dislike simply fails to become law unless Congress affirmatively passes it, and with thousands of rules a year, almost none would. The bill's sponsors framed it as accountability — forcing elected lawmakers to vote on rules instead of leaving them to executive-branch agencies (S2, S3).

how_it_helps.text: No agency regulation could take effect until Congress enacted a bill containing the regulation's exact text, so rules opponents disliked would fail by default rather than requiring a court challenge (S3).

The bill set up an expedited process: regulation bills could not be referred to committee, all points of order were waived, debate was capped at one hour, and a final vote had to happen within 60 calendar days (S3).
Sponsors said the purpose was to end the practice of Congress delegating lawmaking to unelected agency officials and to make elected officials personally responsible for federal rules (S2, S3).
Rules enacted through this process would no longer be treated as agency actions in court, shifting legal fights to the statute itself (S3).

analysis.who_pays: The public pays through protections that would never take effect: rules on air and water pollution, workplace safety, food safety, consumer finance, and drug safety would each need a standalone act of Congress. Given Congress's limited bandwidth, most would simply never happen, and agencies' scientific and technical work would be subject to political veto.

drawbacks.text: Agencies issue thousands of rules each year, most technical and uncontroversial; requiring a signed law for each would make ordinary government regulation nearly impossible, a cost even honest supporters of accountability would have to acknowledge (S3).

The expedited process waives committee review and all points of order and allows only one hour of debate per rule, meaning complex regulations with major health or safety stakes would get less scrutiny than a routine bill (S3).

The exception process in the bill let either House suspend the special procedure by majority vote, so the outcome for any given rule would depend on the political preferences of whichever chamber acted (S3).

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The accountability argument is real — Congress does delegate broad lawmaking power to agencies, and requiring a vote is a coherent constitutional position. But the design swallows the argument: applying it to every binding rule would bring most federal rulemaking to a stop, and the practical winners would be the parties that benefit when rules on pollution, safety, and financial practices never take effect. A narrower version targeting major rules would have carried the accountability argument at far less cost.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary and Rules committees, sent to the Judiciary subcommittee on Commercial and Administrative Law three weeks later, and sat there without a committee vote or floor action until the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Rep. J.D. Hayworth introduced the bill on March 12, 1997, joined by 31 original cosponsors (S3).
It was referred the same day to the House Judiciary Committee and, for relevant provisions, to the House Rules Committee (S5).
On March 20, 1997, it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Commercial and Administrative Law, and no further action was ever recorded (S5).
The bill gathered 67 cosponsors, 65 Republicans and 2 Democrats, but never received a committee markup, a floor vote, or action in the Senate (S4, S5).

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal agencies kept their authority to issue binding rules, and the public kept protections that would otherwise have depended on Congress passing each one. Regulated businesses lost the chance to see most new rules die by default, which is what the bill would have produced.

industries.industry: Regulated industries (manufacturing, energy, finance, and other businesses subject to federal rules)
industries.note: The bill would have made every new federal rule die unless Congress affirmatively passed it, an outcome regulated parties could not achieve through courts or comment periods. The public cost is protections on pollution, safety, and financial practices that would simply never take effect.

Agencies would keep studying and writing rules but lose the power to make them binding without a new law, gutting their core function. Their work, however, is the mechanism through which the public gets the protections at stake.
